{{Short description|Mathematical function}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''p''-adic exponential function}}
In [[mathematics]], particularly [[P-adic analysis|''p''-adic analysis]], the '''''p''-adic exponential function''' is a ''p''-adic analogue of the usual [[exponential function]] on the [[complex numbers]]. As in the complex case, it has an [[inverse function]], named the '''''p''-adic logarithm'''.

==Definition==
The usual exponential function on <math>\mathbb{C}</math> is defined by the infinite series
:<math>\exp(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{z^n}{n!}.</math>
Entirely analogously, one defines the exponential function on <math>\mathbb{C}_p</math>, the completion of the [[algebraic closure]] of <math>\mathbb{Q}_p</math>, by
:<math>\exp_p(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{n!}.</math>
However, unlike exp which converges on all of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, <math>\exp_p</math> only converges on the disc
:<math>|z|_p<p^{-1/(p-1)}.</math>
This is because ''p''-adic series converge if and only if the summands tend to zero, and since the <math>n!</math> in the denominator of each summand tends to make them large ''p''-adically, a small value of ''z'' is needed in the numerator. It follows from [[Legendre's formula]] that if <math>|z|_p < p^{-1/(p-1)}</math> then <math>\frac{z^n}{n!}</math> tends to <math>0</math>, ''p''-adically.

Although the ''p''-adic exponential is sometimes denoted <math>e^x</math>, the [[e (mathematical constant)|number ''e'']] itself has no ''p''-adic analogue. This is because the power series <math>\exp_p(x)</math> does not converge at <math>x=1</math>. It is possible to choose a number <math>e</math> to be a ''p''-th root of <math>\exp_p(p)</math> for <math>p\neq 2</math>,{{efn|or a 4th root of exp<sub>2</sub>(4), for {{nowrap|''p'' {{=}} 2}}}} but there are multiple such roots and there is no canonical choice among them.<ref>{{harvnb|Robert|2000|p=252}}</ref>

==''p''-adic logarithm function==

The power series
:<math>\log_p(1+x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n},</math>
converges for <math>x</math> in <math>\mathbb{C}_p</math> satisfying <math>|x|_p<1</math> and so defines the '''''p''-adic logarithm function''' <math>\log_p(z)</math> for <math>|z-1|_p<1</math> satisfying the usual property <math>\log_p(zw)=\log_p(z)+\log_p(w)</math>. The function <math>\log_p</math> can be extended to all of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>{{SubSup||''p''|×}} (the set of nonzero elements of <math>\mathbb{C}_p</math>) by imposing that it continues to satisfy this last property and setting <math>\log_p(p)=0</math>. Specifically, every element <math>w</math> of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>{{SubSup||''p''|×}} can be written as <math>w=p^r\cdot\zeta\cdot z</math> with <math>r</math> a [[rational number]], <math>\zeta</math> a [[root of unity]], and <math>|z-1|_p<1</math>,<ref>{{harvnb|Cohen|2007|loc=Proposition 4.4.44}}</ref> in which case <math>\log_p(w)=\log_p(z)</math>.{{efn|In factoring ''w'' as above, there is a choice of a root involved in writing ''p<sup>r</sup>'' since ''r'' is rational; however, different choices differ only by multiplication by a root of unity, which gets absorbed into the factor ζ.}} This function on <math>\mathbb{C}</math>{{SubSup||''p''|×}} is sometimes called the '''Iwasawa logarithm''' to emphasize the choice of <math>\log_p(p)=0</math>. In fact, there is an extension of the logarithm from <math>|z-1|_p<1</math> to all of <math>\mathbb{C}</math>{{SubSup||''p''|×}} for each choice of <math>\log_p(p)</math> in <math>\mathbb{C}_p</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Cohen|2007|loc=§4.4.11}}</ref>

==Properties==

If <math>z</math> and <math>w</math> are both in the [[radius of convergence]] for <math>\exp_p</math>, then their sum is too and we have the usual addition formula: <math>\exp_p(z+w)=\exp_p(z)\exp_p(w)</math>.

Similarly if <math>z</math> and <math>w</math> are nonzero elements of <math>\mathbb{C}_p</math> then <math>\log_p(zw)=\log_p(z)+\log_p(w)</math>.

For <math>z</math> in the domain of <math>\exp_p</math>, we have <math>\exp_p(\log_p(1+z))=1+z</math> and <math>\log_p(\exp_p(z))=z</math>.

The roots of the Iwasawa logarithm <math>\log_p(z)</math> are exactly the elements of <math>\mathbb{C}_p</math> of the form <math>p^r\cdot\zeta</math> where <math>r</math> is a rational number and <math>\zeta</math> is a root of unity.<ref>{{harvnb|Cohen|2007|loc=Proposition 4.4.45}}</ref>

Note that there is no analogue in <math>\mathbb{C}_p</math> of [[Euler's identity]], <math>e^{2\pi i}=1</math>.  This is a corollary of [[Strassmann's theorem]].

Another major difference to the situation in <math>\mathbb{C}</math> is that the domain of convergence of <math>\exp_p</math> is much smaller than that of <math>\log_p</math>.  A modified exponential function &mdash; the [[Artin–Hasse exponential]] &mdash; can be used instead which converges on <math>|z|_p<1</math>.
